Memory.value: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together

vignette:
Liam, a 29-year-old Coast Guard boatswain's mate, has always prided himself on his steady hands and clear head, qualities essential for navigating the treacherous waters off the coast. For seven years, his life has been one of disciplined routines and the tangible reality of sea, wind, and steel. Six months ago, while walking home from a rare late night out with friends, that reality was shattered. Two men emerged from an unlit alleyway, one moving behind him while the other blocked his path. He remembers the sudden, sharp pressure at his back, the glint of something metallic under the streetlight, and the rough scrape of the pavement against his cheek after he was shoved to the ground. The entire event unfolded in a disorienting silence, a blur of motion without clear words, ending with his wallet gone and the sound of footsteps fading into the night.

In the months that followed, Liam returned to his duties, to the familiar rhythm of watches and drills on the cutter. He went through the motions, his performance unwavering, but a profound internal shift had taken place. The incident occupies a strange space in his mind. His memory of the event does not exist as a coherent story he can recount. Instead, it comes to him in disconnected pieces that refuse to fit together: the silver flash of a watch on a wrist, the specific smell of damp asphalt, the feeling of his jacket being pulled tight across his shoulders. These are like isolated frames from a film he can't rewind or fast-forward.

At other times, a sequence of what happened will play out in his mind with stark clarity. He can see the man’s face, the frayed cuff of his sleeve, the pattern of cracks in the sidewalk. During these moments, however, he feels a profound and unsettling numbness. It is as if he is watching a stranger being robbed, a detached observer to a scene that has no emotional weight or personal connection to him. He feels nothing at all.

When his girlfriend, Chloe, or his shipmates ask what happened, Liam finds himself at a loss. He can list the facts—he was mugged, they took his wallet, he was unhurt—but he cannot seem to put the frightening core of the event into words. The terror he knows he must have felt remains locked away, inaccessible to language. The story feels hollow when he tells it, a second-hand account of something that happened to someone else, leaving those who care about him confused and him feeling profoundly isolated.

He came to therapy at Chloe’s urging. She had noticed a quietness in him, a new distance he couldn't explain. Liam himself is not sure what he hopes to achieve. He isn't having nightmares or flashbacks in the way he's seen in movies. He is simply carrying a memory that feels broken, an incomplete file in his mind that he can neither delete nor fully open. His primary hope is to understand why the memory of the worst moment of his life feels like it doesn't belong to him.
